title: Adding time-constant component hazard ratios mispredicted a combination's RMST when effects were delayed or follow-up differed
question: When two components have different time profiles of effect and their trials differ in follow-up, does adding their time-constant hazard ratios predict the combination's RMST, and does a piecewise extension fix it?
design: Trials of each component against control with constant, jointly delayed, or delayed-versus-waning effects and equal or unequal follow-up; stratified Cox with time-constant or piecewise component effects predicting the combination's 3-year RMST difference. 4 cells, 500 replicates each.
answer: No. With both component effects delayed, adding time-constant hazard ratios overstated the combination's 3-year RMST gain by 0.055 years (truth 0.405, coverage 0.88); a piecewise model reduced the bias to 0.017. With delayed and waning components and follow-up of 1.5 versus 3 years, the time-constant prediction was biased by -0.102 (coverage 0.82) and the piecewise model by -0.072 (coverage 0.91), because neither can learn a late effect the shorter trial never observed. With equal follow-up and effects summing to a constant, the time-constant model was accurate.
findings: Registered rule: neither model nominal where it mattered (piecewise 0.906 at unequal follow-up).
A constant hazard ratio moves benefit earlier than a delayed one, and RMST credits early benefit.
Constant effects: both models unbiased with coverage 0.93 to 0.94.
not_answered: Two single-component trials rather than a component network; no disconnection or population adjustment; one piecewise extension; one horizon. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: 3-year RMST difference of the component combination versus control
